description: We are a team of university students taking on the Field Shift challenge. Farmers face shifting temperatures, less predictable rainfall, and declining soil health, which makes choosing crop rotations harder every year. We plan to combine NASA Earth observation data with USDA crop and soil records to help farmers compare rotation options that protect their soil and adapt to changing conditions. Our team brings experience in software engineering, web development, AI, and data visualization.
summary:
Fieldproof is a free web app for dryland wheat farmers in eastern Washington. They keep hearing they should diversify, but switching a field is a bet with the family's income. Before they make it, they want to know one thing: would a new crop actually pay here?

You find your field on a map and answer four quick questions. Fieldproof then runs 21 years of NASA weather and USDA harvest and price records for that spot. You see what each crop would have earned per acre in a normal year and in a dry year, next to what you grow now. At our Ritzville sample farm, peas lose money at today's prices. Canola might pay more, but it loses money in dry years.

So instead of saying "switch," Fieldproof suggests a small test: 12 acres of the new crop beside 12 acres of wheat, with the most you could lose spelled out. NASA satellites add each field's history. HLS shows whether it grew a crop or rested every year since 2015, and ECOSTRESS shows how hot it ran in summer. You can compare several crops at once. And because the same public records exist for every US farming county, Fieldproof can grow well beyond Washington.
details:
WHY WE BUILT IT

In 2021, Adams County, Washington had its driest spring in 45 years of NASA records, and the state's wheat harvest fell by almost half. Farmers out there are told to diversify all the time. Try peas, try canola. But nobody can tell them whether it would pay on their own ground, and a wrong guess on a whole field can cost tens of thousands of dollars. So most of them never try.

WHAT IT DOES

You find your farm by town, by section and township, or by "I'm at my field," and click your field on Washington's official field outlines. We fill in four answers you can change: what you grow now, whether you irrigate, the crop you're curious about, and what matters most to you (for example, steady income in bad years).

Then you get one answer in plain dollars per acre. At the Ritzville sample farm, what you grow now makes about $14 an acre in a normal year. Adding peas loses about $22. Canola might make about $38, but it loses about $27 in a dry year. Fieldproof doesn't tell you to switch. It gives you the smallest safe test: 12 acres of peas next to 12 acres of wheat. That costs about $1,650 in a normal year, and about $4,400 at worst, if the peas fail completely.

It's also honest about what it doesn't know. It replays the past to check its own advice, nine times over. When 21 years of records can't settle the question, it says "Not enough history to prove it here" instead of pretending.

HOW IT WORKS

For every year from 2005 to 2025, the engine works out harvest × price − costs for each rotation, in today's dollars. Harvests and prices come from USDA, and costs come from WSU and University of Idaho farm budgets. It checks 55 crops for whether they can grow there at all. The weather sliders ("what if springs get drier?") give more weight to real past years that looked like that, so no harvest is ever invented.

THE NASA DATA

- NASA POWER: 21 years of daily rain and heat at the farm.

- NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6: what eight climate models say about springs to come.

- NASA HLS (Landsat and Sentinel-2, 30 m): we processed it into a crop-or-rest record for 14,932 fields across three counties. You can press play and watch the wheat-and-rest rhythm of the whole region from 2015 to 2025.

- NASA ECOSTRESS on the Space Station: summer ground heat per field. Resting fields run 5 to 12 °F hotter than growing ones.

- NASA MODIS: the zoomed-out view.

MORE THAN ONE CROP, MORE THAN ONE FARM

You can compare up to four crops side by side, always next to what you grow now. Every field in Washington gets a "can it grow here?" check for 55 crops, so thirsty crops on dryland simply say "Needs irrigation here." The money answers cover two sample farms today, each in a very different climate:

- Ritzville in Adams County is dry country with about 12 inches of rain a year. Its rotations use wheat, peas and canola.

- Pullman in Whitman County gets about 20 inches. Its rotations use wheat, chickpeas, lentils, peas, barley and canola.

WHERE IT GOES NEXT

Nothing in Fieldproof is tied to one place:

- The data covers far more ground. NASA POWER, HLS and ECOSTRESS cover the whole planet. USDA publishes county harvests and prices for every farming county in the US.

- New counties are a data job, not a rebuild. Adding one means loading its records and a local farm budget. The engine and the app stay the same.

- The next steps: more of eastern Washington, starting with Grant County; then dryland areas facing the same question, like Oregon, Idaho and the Great Plains; and later, field-level harvest estimates from HLS greenness, so the money answer reflects each field and not just its county.

TOOLS

- The app: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server, hosted on GitHub Pages. MapLibre draws the globe and the field map.

- Satellite processing: Python and GDAL.

- Tests: 347 automated tests, plus browser tests.

WHAT WE CARED ABOUT

- Plain words and dollars first. No dashboards.

- Access: it works on a phone, by keyboard and with a screen reader, with no account needed.

- Every number has a source you can see. Where data is thin, it says so. For example, there are no county canola harvests for Adams County, so it uses Washington averages and tells you.

- No AI inside the product. We used AI coding tools to help build it, but every number on screen traces back to a public record.
